newsitem.title: UK: London precious metals ease after gold hits $350.
newsitem.headline: London precious metals ease after gold hits $350.

text.p: Gold prices eased on Tuesday after they ran up to hit resistance around $350 an ounce, at the firmest for a month, during a rally that began late last week and extended through Monday.
Dealers said technical charts still looked optimistic, despite a lower London morning fixing at $347.30, down from $348.20.
But the market had slipped after it briefly broke key resistance of $350 to reach $350.40 on Monday.
Gains from a lower platform of $340 last week were helped by the dollar's fall against the yen, which stirred Japanese interest, and also by the impact of sharp rises in platinum and palladium.
Perceptions that new central bank gold sales may not be imminent also helped gold, but dealers were nonetheless looking for a correction.

"The feeling is that we may try and find support. The 100-day moving average is $351. That's going to be a major resistance level," said one. But he added that if platinum and palladium advanced again, gold and silver would also benefit.
"The dollar/yen has stabilised. That will start wearing off as far as the effect on gold is concerned," he added.
Technical analyst Karen Jones of Credit Suisse First Boston said gold could drop to $345 or even $343.50 without losing its sparkle on the charts. But she saw resistance at $354-$355.
Even in India where the wedding season has pushed gold demand to its peak, buyers were shunning higher prices.
Platinum and palladium also surrendered some gains after high prices attracted fresh lending to a tight forward market where one-month palladium was lent at 20 percent from 25.
A Russian official's comments on Monday that a decree to permit delayed exports of platinum group metals to Japan to resume had been signed cooled the market's ardour.
But heavy involvement of speculative funds, especially in palladium, meant it could rally again.
A dealer said the Russians had not been precise yet about when they would resume exports and in what volume.
But sources in Japan's electronics industry, a major end user of Russian palladium, said they were stepping up efforts to switch to cheaper and more stable substitues such as nickel.
Platinum, which came close to $400 an ounce on Monday was quoted at $388.75/$389.75 on Tuesday. Palladium traded $4.75 lower at $168.75/$169.75.
